en: Choose One Height: White Pagoda Hill, Lanshan, or Wuquan Mountain
zh: 从哪一处看全城：白塔山、兰山或五泉山
ja: 街をどこから見るか：白塔山・蘭山・五泉山

p.src: Do not rank the three hills before looking at the day already planned. If Zhongshan Bridge is still ahead, choose White Pagoda Hill and join the bridge, river, and two banks in one walk. Choose Lanshan and Santai Pavilion to see why Lanzhou stretches east-west through a narrow valley. Choose Wuquan Mountain to walk among shade, named springs, courtyards, and historic buildings. The figure shows the compact pagoda precinct and terraced park on White Pagoda Hill. Its advantage is direct contact with the central route, not greater height. Pick one place, decide what you want to see, and only then check weather, access, and the return.

caption.zh: 七级白塔立在紧凑塔院与层叠公园之上。到入口再选下层台地或完整登高，不把所有屋顶看成同一时代。
caption.ja: 七層の白塔が小さな境内と段状の公園の上に立つ。入口で下段までか白塔寺の境内までかを選び、すべての屋根を同時代とは見なさない。
caption.en: The seven-level pagoda rises above a compact precinct and terraced park. Choose the lower terraces or full climb at the entrance, and do not treat every roof as one historical layer.

p.src: This diagram shows the choice, not turn-by-turn navigation. The Yellow River crosses the middle. White Pagoda Hill rises at the north end of Zhongshan Bridge; Wuquan Mountain lies south of the city at the north foot of the Gaolan range; Santai Pavilion on Lanshan sits higher to the south. Turn around at the lower terraces or pagoda precinct on White Pagoda Hill, at the high point whose access you confirmed on Lanshan, or after one confirmed open section of courtyards and spring paths at Wuquan. No solid line joins Wuquan to Lanshan, and no cableway, bus, or walking time is printed. Check visibility first, then wind or rain and the path surface, the stairs or transfer, and the descent. If one check fails, keep a city-level route.

caption.zh: 白塔山接中山桥与两岸，兰山看河谷形，五泉山走园林与古建；三处只选一处，再核对天气、道路和回程。
caption.ja: 白塔山は中山橋と両岸、蘭山は河谷の形、五泉山は園林と古建築を見る。一か所だけ選び、天候、経路、帰路を確かめる。
caption.en: White Pagoda Hill joins the bridge and two banks, Lanshan reads the valley form, and Wuquan combines park and historic buildings. Choose one, then check weather, access, and the return.

p.src: White Pagoda Hill fits directly after Zhongshan Bridge. The park begins at the north end, so no second vehicle is needed. Decide at the entrance whether to stop at the lower terraces or continue to the compact precinct of the seven-level, eight-sided pagoda. The lower level already explains the bridge, river, and park axis; turning there is a complete visit. Continue only after checking the route open that day, wet or icy steps, access to the precinct, and daylight for the descent. Chapter 4 covers the floating bridge, iron bridge, and park chronology. If that route is already complete, White Pagoda Hill is complete too. Do not climb it again merely because it appears in this comparison.

p.src: Choose Lanshan to read the valley, not to collect a night-view photograph. Near Santai Pavilion, find the Yellow River crossing the city, then see how buildings, rail, and roads extend mainly east-west between the northern and southern heights. The figure puts Santai Pavilion and the valley in one view. The four guides provide foreground scale; look past them to the river and the city's east-west form. If low cloud or haze already hides the river before departure, choose Wuquan's courtyards or keep the city-level route. If the view disappears only after arrival, descend as planned instead of changing hills.

caption.zh: 到三台阁，看的不是一幢高楼，而是兰州如何沿黄河谷向东西展开；出发前仍要核对能见度、上山路和回程。
caption.ja: 三台閣で見るのは一棟の高い建物ではなく、蘭州が黄河の谷に沿って東西へ延びる形である。出発前に視界、上り道、帰路を確かめる。
caption.en: At Santai Pavilion, read not one skyline building but the way Lanzhou extends east-west along the Yellow River valley. Check visibility, access, and the return before setting out.

p.src: Treat the ascent and descent as one booking decision. On the day, search current maps and official notices for “Lanshan Scenic Area” and “Santai Pavilion”, then confirm the entrance or pickup point, whether the service is one-way or return, how much walking remains, the last usable connection, and a normal route back to the city after dark. A June 2026 tourism itinerary mentioned taxi or cableway access. A separate notice described bus 750 only for increased service from May 1 to 5; it is not evidence of a year-round route. A driver willing to go uphill does not guarantee a return booking. If the only descent plan is “work it out later,” do not set out.

p.src: The Santai high point is recorded at 2,129.6 metres, but the pavilion in front of you is not a Ming building preserved unchanged. Local records describe repeated loss and rebuilding; the present 26-metre Santai Pavilion on the central platform was rebuilt in 1983-1984. That distinction makes Lanshan easier to read. People have long used the high ground to look over the city; pavilions were lost and rebuilt, while hill greening changed the surrounding landscape. There is no need to memorise a list of old scenic names. Align the river, two heights, and east-west direction from Chapter 1 with the terrain below. Once those three elements match, descend.

p.src: The subject at Wuquan Mountain is not a distant skyline. It is the sequence of park paths, trees, walls, and roofs rising across the slope. Use the layers in the figure for orientation: lower paths offer places to pause or turn back, courtyards and halls occupy the middle slope, and only then do higher paths continue. The four guides stand low in the scene, giving scale to the eaves, steps, and tree crowns. What matters is recognising how far the open route extends. Visit one courtyard that is open, read its entrance panel, and then decide whether to continue. There is no need to complete all 24 historic buildings or groups.

caption.zh: 五泉山要由下往上读院落、屋顶、树荫与坡度；走完一个层级就折返，也是一段完整的游览。
caption.ja: 五泉山は下から中庭、屋根、木陰、勾配を順に読む。一段だけ歩いて引き返しても、一つの散策として完結する。
caption.en: Read Wuquan upward through courtyards, roofs, shade, and slope. Turning back after one level still makes a complete visit.

p.src: Wuquan Mountain takes its name from five springs: Ganlu, Juyue, Mozi, Hui, and Meng. Use those names first to recognise signs. The surviving group developed from Yuan-period construction through Ming, Qing, and Republican-era additions and repairs, creating a hillside mix of shrines, temples, and garden space. The complex received national-level protected heritage status in 2013. Nine heritage buildings reopened after conservation work in 2023, but that reopening does not guarantee every doorway today. Read current notices and barriers at the entrance, then take one open branch. Do not cross a barrier to find a spring or assume that spring water is safe to drink. If a hall is under repair, go around it and let the conservation boundary define the route.

p.src: Check the Chengguan hourly forecast and site notices before leaving; at the gate, look for low cloud, wind in the trees, standing water, and local announcements. Lightning, heavy rain, strong wind, ice, mud, or closure cancels the climb. In the 2026 flood season, Wuquan's procedure included monitoring, broadcast clearance, and temporary closure. For a step-free route, confirm not only where a car or cableway stops but also any slopes, steps, narrow gates, or equipment out of service beyond it. Knee or ankle pain, a heavy bag, or low daylight also means turning back. Use the riverfront, museum, or a teahouse instead.

p.src: Once you descend from the chosen turnaround, the day's hill visit is complete. White Pagoda Hill returns to Zhongshan Bridge or a north-bank exit; Lanshan uses the city return confirmed before departure; Wuquan leaves by the same route or another exit currently open. Do not cross the city after descending to chase sunset from a second hill. Give the remaining time to a normal meal, dropping things at the hotel, or reaching the station early. If weather deteriorates during the outing, return to the city-level route rather than switching hills. Each height serves a different purpose; walking one is enough.
